newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb hardliners prepare way for possible coup.
newsitem.headline: Serb hardliners prepare way for possible coup.

text.p: Bosnian Serb hardliners accused President Biljana Plavsic of endangering the security of Serb territory in an attack that appeared to prepare the ground for her possible overthrow.

Hardliners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic used official television and radio on Sunday to poetry Plavsic as a traitor who was threatening the future of the Bosnia's Serb republic.

The Bosnian Serb SRNA news agency, under the strict control of Karadzic loyalists, said it had obtained a letter written by the army commander demanding Plavsic consult the military "before taking any further decision in this situation".
Western envoys expressed serious doubts about the authenticity of the letter as army generals had vowed to stay out of the confrontation three days ago.
They said the report, combined with moves to strip Plavsic of defence powers and rewrite laws to enable her recall, indicated that Karadzic and his associates were threatening to stage a coup.

Plavsic, who has gained international support in her battle with Karadzic's allies, has dissolved the Bosnian Serb assembly and called for elections on September 1. But the hardliners have ignored her decision.
The letter carried by SRNA said Plavsic's order to dissolve parliament had brought Bosnia's Serb entity "to the brink of ruin".
The report alleged that the rival Moslem-Croat federation military was mobilising and said the army reserved the right to defend the "constitutional order".
There was no immediate response from Plavsic in the northwest town of Banja Luka, where nervous police who have sided with her are guarding presidential offices.

Although Plavsic is a nationalist ideologue, Western governments say she has shown a willingness to cooperate with the Dayton peace accords to obtain reconstruction aid and investment for Serb territory.
Karadzic, forced to step down last year due to his status as a suspect indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, anointed Plavsic in the belief she would prove an obedient successor.
But Plavsic has demanded investigations into alleged corruption linked to Karadzic and his main ally, Momcilo Krasjinik, the Serb member of the collective presidency.
Her detailed charges embarrassed Karadzic's party and struck a chord among former soldiers and refugees living in abject poverty.
The conflict has reinforced antagonism between Banja Luka, the largest town in Serb territory, and the civilian leadership residing in the mountain village of Pale.

The NATO-led peace force has deployed additional troops in and around Banja Luka to prevent a possible clash between Plavsic's supporters, which include military police, and Karadzic's security units.
Plavsic's opponents accused NATO of ordering British soldiers to help guard her building last week.
Army chief General Pero Colic arrived at the presidential offices on Sunday but local media said it was unclear if Plavsic received him.
Colic was appointed commander last year after Karadzic's party purged the army of senior officers who had accused the civilian leadership of wartime corruption.
Diplomats said U.S. and European governments planned to keep up support for Plavsic and to demand Karadzic's party allow her access to official television.

The chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, Gen. John Shalikashvili, said on Sunday that alleged war criminals from the Bosnian conflict still at large presented an obstacle to peace in the region and must be arrested.

"I would tell you that war criminals have been recognised from the very beginning as being a great impediment to the Dayton (peace) agreement," the general said in an interview on CNN's "Late Edition."
The Los Angeles Times on Sunday reported that the Special Forces and the CIA had prepared a secret plan to capture Karadzic.
Quoting U.S. intelligence sources, the Times said the plan was a response to Washington's growing concern that Karadzic was a major threat to long-term peace in former Yugoslavia.
